title: Kent: Words of Estimative Probability
description: Catalogue data for the Kent visual. The page does not fetch this file: the scale, examples, glossary and messages are inlined in index.html, and a test keeps them equal. Every probability comes from the visitor; simulated readers are generated on the device and are never measurements.

glossary.title: Proposition
glossary.text: What might happen: the claim being judged, stated so that it will later be clearly true or false.

glossary.title: Probability
glossary.text: How likely the proposition is, from 0% (impossible) to 100% (certain).

glossary.title: Word
glossary.text: A linguistic encoding of probability. Words are coarse: many numbers hide behind one word.

glossary.title: Kent band
glossary.text: The probability region Kent conventionally attached to a word, such as 63–87% for “probable”.

glossary.title: Kent anchor
glossary.text: The representative point of a Kent band, such as 75% for “probable”. Kent never meant the word to be exactly that number.

glossary.title: Analytic confidence
glossary.text: How strongly the available evidence supports the probability assessment. It is not a second probability and is never combined with one.

glossary.title: Probability vs confidence
glossary.text: 72% with low confidence and 72% with high confidence are the same probability on a different footing: the first could move a lot with new evidence.

glossary.title: Low-confidence estimates
glossary.text: A low-confidence estimate still needs a number. Low confidence says the number may move, not that it is near 50%.

glossary.title: Odds representation
glossary.text: Odds compare happening with not happening: 75% is 3 : 1 on, 25% is 3 : 1 against.

glossary.title: Probability ↔ odds
glossary.text: odds = p / (1 − p); p = odds / (1 + odds). Kent wrote “65 to 35 in favour”.

glossary.title: Natural frequency
glossary.text: The same probability as a count: 72% is about 7 times in 10 similar situations.

glossary.title: Complement
glossary.text: The chance it does not happen: 100% minus the probability. 72% leaves 28%.

glossary.title: Evidence
glossary.text: Observations informing the assessment. Here they are notes only: nothing scores them into a number. The analyst owns the judgment.

glossary.title: Updating
glossary.text: New evidence should move an estimate. The size of the move, in percentage points, is part of the story.

glossary.title: Decision threshold
glossary.text: The probability at which an action becomes worthwhile. With cost C of acting needlessly and L of failing to act, act when p ≥ C / (C + L).

glossary.title: Outcome
glossary.text: What eventually occurred: yes, no or ambiguous. Ambiguous outcomes are kept but not scored.

glossary.title: Calibration
glossary.text: The relationship between stated probabilities and observed frequencies: of all your 70% forecasts, about 70% should happen.

glossary.title: Brier score
glossary.text: (p − o)², averaged over resolved forecasts, where o is 1 if it happened and 0 if not. Lower is better; 0 is perfect.

glossary.title: Simulated readers
glossary.text: Readers generated on this device from a broad spread, to demonstrate that decoders differ. Never measurements.

glossary.title: Your uncertainty range
glossary.text: Your own plausible range for the probability itself. It is not a Kent word band.

glossary.title: False precision
glossary.text: 72.384729% claims more than any real judgment can support. The value is kept; the display rounds to 72%.

glossary.title: Sherman Kent
glossary.text: Kent ran the CIA's Board of National Estimates and in 1964 proposed agreeing on the vocabulary of probability first.

messages.nan: That is not a number: type a probability such as 72.
messages.claim: Write the claim first: what exactly might happen?
messages.costs: Costs must be numbers of zero or more.
messages.noCosts: At least one of the two costs must be above zero.
messages.unknown: There is no forecast with that id.
messages.resolved: This forecast is already resolved: record a correction instead.
messages.outcome: An outcome is yes, no or ambiguous.
messages.orderLo: The low end of your range must not be above your best estimate.
messages.orderHi: The high end of your range must not be below your best estimate.
